I was sitting at a table across from my best friend for the first time in three years. The coffee shop was mostly empty and neither of us ordered anything. In college, Spencer had been my roommate. For the longest time he was the closest friend I had ever had. Hanging out with him was the only reason I could stand my life at the time. He was always there for me in every aspect of my life and then suddenly he just…wasn’t. I don’t remember the specific reason that he left, I didn’t understand it then either. It was like he dropped off the face of the earth. The only evidence I received contrary to my initial fear that he had died, was a single phone call.

In this phone call Spencer assured me he was alive and well, and that he would be out of contact with me for a very long time. In fact, that was all he had said. Three years had passed since then and the man sitting before me had drastically changed. I used to envy Spencer for his good looks and his suave way with women. Given his long blonde hair that always sat perfectly without any effort, his deep blue eyes, and the relaxed easygoing attitude he carried in everything he did, Spencer was your stereotypical teen girl heartthrob.

But now, despite his youth, Spencer’s short hair was streaked with the grey sheen of constant stress. He was still tall and lean with a firm jaw line and warm smile, but the carefree light in his eyes had been replaced with the unmistakable look of perpetual worry. He wore a long sleeved collared shirt, faded jeans, and worn leather boots. Resting upon the floor next to his feet was a thick black briefcase.

In truth, I had begun to believe I’d never see him again. That was, until I received an email from an address I didn’t recognize. The subject bar had read, “Urgent. I need your help.” Initially, I assumed it was just a spam email. But then I actually read the contents. Therein, Spencer apologized for his absence, explained that he needed my help with something very urgent, and instructed me to meet him at the coffee shop that used to be our favorite place to get lunch. He pressed that the matter was of “life or death” importance.

He never specified a date or time to meet him, but when I walked into the shop he was already sitting at a table. Oddly enough, I wasn’t bitter at all for being abandoned. Spencer was the kind of friend that you found yourself begrudgingly unable to hate. Whatever the man had become, he was still irrevocably my best friend and I was willing to help him in any way I could. His look was that of a man on business rather than a desire to reunite, so I cut the formalities and greeted him by saying, “Whatever you need me to do, I agree to it in advance.”

That put a smile back into his weary eyes. “It’s good to see you,” he said, “I’m sorry for disappearing for so long.” His tone was sincere, but his words seemed rehearsed in preparation for my resentment. He would find none. “Forget all that,” I responded, “Tell me what I can do to help you.” The worry returned to his eyes. “I appreciate your eagerness to help, but you have to understand what I’m asking of you. This is serious. This is dangerous. I’m not joking when I tell you there is a good chance that we could both die. Are you really sure that you want to be a part of this?”

I didn’t weigh his warning long before confirming my original answer. It gave Spencer a strange sad smile. He furrowed his brow like he was unsure what to say next. He then leaned in and whispered to me, “I…I need you to help me kill my ex-wife.”

I refused to offer him a response, choosing instead to stare at him blankly.

“Listen, you know me. You know I wouldn’t ask you for help like this if it wasn’t important. I have to stop her. We have to stop her. We have to stop her or else more people will die.”

I could hear the desperation in his voice. “What are you talking about? I said I would help you, but you can’t expect me to just help you kill someone. If you think your ex-wife is dangerous you need to go to the police.” “The police?” he snapped, half scoffing. He seemed offended by the very suggestion. “I’ve been trying to track Charlotte down for almost three years now, and not once have the police been anything but a nuisance to me when I sought them out for help.”

His frustration wasn’t making me any less confused. “Please, just start from the beginning.” He paused. “I’m not superstitious,” he began, “I never was. I’ve always strived to find a logical explanation for the things I can’t understand, but my experiences since the last time we met have thrown my world passed all rationality. I can’t deny my senses, and I’ve learned there are things in this world that are beyond explanation. However, I’ll try my best.” His tone echoed the pain of harsh memory and regret. I thought she was my wife,” he answered, “I loved her. I would have given my life for her, until she actually tried to take it from me.” His fingers nervously fiddled with a packet of sugar. “Why can’t the police help you catch her?” I interjected. “Because the person that I thought was my wife isn’t a person. She’s a monster… Some creature, or demon, or entity. Whatever she is, I know she’s a being of pure evil.” I might have laughed if it weren’t for the look on his face. “It all started on our honeymoon,” he continued, “On that day she led me to a secluded barn in the middle of nowhere. I never even questioned where she was taking me; I would have followed her anywhere.” His quiet chuckle was harrowing. “She was the perfect girl. Black hair, blue eyes, and the perfect personality. I mean, we never fought once. Spending time with her made me the happiest I’d ever been. I cried like a baby on our wedding day…” His voice lowered as his face darkened. “But it was all a lie. All of it.”

What do you mean? She didn’t love you?” I asked.

“You don’t understand,” He said, “None of it happened. The day I thought I married Charlotte was the day that I met her.” He could tell I was still not getting it. “She isn’t human! Every memory I have of her isn’t mine. She planted it there. That’s how it gets you. I don’t know how she does it but she fools your mind. She convinces you that you see a beautiful person, a person you’ve known for years, someone you love, someone you trust. I’m far from the first person she’s lured in, and despite my best efforts, I haven’t been the last. However, I do think I am the first person to escape it.” Spencer’s words were too earnest for him to simply be insane.

“How did you survive?” I quietly asked him. “What did she do to you?”

“She…took me to an old barn late at night.” It was then that I realized how badly he was trembling. “When she brought me in there I thought she wanted to...well…you know. But when we went inside she locked the door behind us and trapped me there.” The more Spencer tried to calm himself the worse he shuddered. He was clearly hesitant to continue. “I saw her…I saw what she really looks like. She can make herself look like anyone for all I know, but it’s all an illusion. As soon as she trapped me in there the facade ended. It was dark in there, but by the light of a weak flashlight I saw my wife’s smiling face melt away” As he lost himself in recollection, Spencer’s expression was ghastly. “Her clothes and her skin…they just…liquefied. Charlotte’s flesh tightened and contracted until she became a visage of contorted leathery grotesqueness. She twisted into a mummified hairless corpse whose features gave no hint of a defining gender. Its limbs and fingers looked elongated. Its bones stretched the thin skin like they were too lengthy for the body to hold them. Every one of her ribs jutted out. When its wrinkled lips pulled back, its teeth looked unnaturally long.” Spencer had stopped attempting to subdue his shaking at this point. “Charlotte was still smiling the whole time. Only now her once charming smile had become an unnerving grin. But the worst part was the eyes. They sunk deep into its skull and turned black. But they weren’t just black, they were dark pits. Almost like…you know how light can’t escape from a black hole? They were darker than that. Darker than anything I’ve ever seen, than anything I can imagine. It wasn’t just a cold abyss, they defied all color. When you looked in them you saw…nothingness. That’s the best I can describe them.” He looked ready to cry. “But when I looked into those eyes I felt it. I felt it eating me. I could feel it all, my life force, being steadily sapped away by her eyes. It was devouring my soul, draining all my energy away. I could only stand, frozen in fear, as each second took more away of what made me human. She only stood there as well. Then gnarled fingers reached out at me. When Charlotte held out her arms, like she wanted to embrace me, I panicked. Exhausted, I ran at the door, the wall, anywhere. In a frantic craze I pounded, kicked and clawed at the walls of my prison like a rat caught in a house fire. I thought of trying to attack her, but I was too afraid. And the closer I got to her, the faster my stamina was leeched away. It felt like all the light that keeps me alive was slowly sucked into the void and I was helplessly watching it swallow me." "Either pure blind luck or divine intervention found me that day. I was able to pry a few boards loose in the termite eaten corner of the barn and wriggle my way free. With what little strength I had left, I ran. I fled without stopping to look back.” His eyes wandered from mine as he told his story. He wasn’t at the table anymore, he was in his past. “She didn’t follow me. And I know that, because I could hear her wail. I don’t think it moved from that spot, it just howled that haunting screech I still hear in my nightmares. It was a long droning inhalation like a sickly person struggling to gasp for breath. Like she was trying to suck me back into her decrepit embrace and whither my life away. Again, Spencer shuddered at his own description. “Since that day I have been unable to get a full night’s sleep. I doubt I will ever feel fully energetic again and it’s all because of what she took from me. Charlotte didn’t kill me, but she left me a broken man. We need to stop her before she lures in someone else. I can’t live my life with that thing still out there doing to others what she did to me.”

For a moment, we sat in utter silence. I didn’t have a clue what to say, but I believed him; All of it. You learn to trust the man who saved your life the time you overdosed in your dorm room. That being said, the only thing that shocked me more than his story was how well I was taking it.

“So how do we stop her?” I finally said. “If she can look like anyone and make you think that you know her, how do we even find her? How could we manage to kill her?”

Spencer bit his lip and eyed the briefcase I had forgotten lay at his feet. “For almost three years my life has been completely dedicated to researching, tracking, and killing Charlotte. I started by looking for her previous victims. I checked police records, missing person reports, and unsolved kidnappings. I read every book on myths and legends I could find, just pouring over page after page for any clue to get me closer to the answers I needed. When I was able to muster the courage, I went back to the abandoned barn only to find her missing without a trace. In all this time I still have learned very little about her, but the few bits of information I have found have been useful. Her pattern of killing seems to be a lure and trap technique. She gets inside your head until you trust her. Then she leads you to some web she has prepared in an isolated area. I think it’s because she takes a long time to complete her feeding.

Eventually my hunt brought me to India. I believe that may be the land Charlotte came from. That is where I learned just how old she is. Charlotte has been doing this for centuries, perhaps millennia. Originally her lair was a more permanent location; large caves became the tomb for countless villagers. But the rise of mankind has forced her to resort to more discreet methods. Now, she rarely stays in the same place for long and seldom uses the same lair for more than one person. In most cases the found remains of the victim, if any, are nothing but brittle bones. However, in one particular case, two bodies were left behind with the process of consumption unfinished.

One body looked like a malnourished skeleton just moments away from starving to death, the other was a stiff mass of dry skin that looked as though someone had extracted all traces of moisture from it. I saw the pictures and the second body was the spitting image of the creature I saw in the barn. The gruesome scene had to have been the result of Charlotte leaving in a hurry. Why? I can’t say. But this evidence leads me to believe that not only can Charlotte be killed, but she fears humans capable of doing it.”

“You still haven’t answered my question.” I finally interjected. “How do you intend to kill her?”

Spencer carefully picked up his briefcase and laid it on the table. “This is why I asked you to come here,” He replied, “It’ll take two people to use it. I did a lot of things I’m not proud of to get what’s in this briefcase, so I’d appreciate it if you didn’t ask.”

I reached out to open it until Spencer’s glare shot me down. “Don’t you dare,” he warned. “It’s only going to work once, and I don’t think you want to use it until we find her. I can’t tell you how it works; I can’t even tell you what it is. I swore on my honor I wouldn’t let the secret of its power fall into the wrong hands. So that means the fewer people who know what it is, the better. All you need to know is that if we have this with us when we find Charlotte, and you do exactly what I say when the right time arrives, we’ll be able to stop her once and for all."

All of my understanding of reality had changed dramatically, yet I was taking it all surprisingly well. “Well then how do we begin? Do you even have an idea where we could find her?”

Spencer slid the secret weapon from the table and looked around suspiciously as though he were protecting his own child. “Ironically, my chase has led me around the globe only to take me right back to where I started,” he replied, “Predicting her movements has been difficult, but Charlotte may be getting sloppy. A girl from a town not far from here went missing about six months ago. I’m confident that Charlotte’s current location is not far from the area and that she’s planning on repeating the same pattern for a new victim. I don’t have a car here so I was hoping you can drive.” I nodded. “Then I’ve had enough of sitting around here.” He decided. “I know this is a lot to take in at once, but I’m finally so close. I can’t afford to wait any longer. We can start whenever you’re ready.”

One trip to a coffee shop and everything you thought you knew about the world is different. I even started to find courage I didn’t know I had. “Let’s begin” I announced.

After sorting out the directions and exact means of getting there, Spencer and I began to journey to the home of the missing girl Hailey. Along the way Spencer explained that allegedly, Hailey randomly came home one day with a new boyfriend, and shortly thereafter she ran away with him. Despite the situation, it was good to be spending time with Spencer again. The formula of our relationship hadn’t changed since we were struggling to pass calculus. Spencer was always so sure of himself and driven, while I was always needing him to keep me motivated.

It didn’t surprise me that Spencer was able to get this far by himself. For as long as I’ve known him, it’s like he had his whole life figured out. If you needed someone to help you plan and prepare for something, Spencer was the guy you went to. To put it simply, he was a leader and I was the follower. And I never really thought there was anything wrong with that. I would never have had the initiative or conviction to track Charlotte down or figure out how she could be killed but that doesn’t mean I can’t help.

After a couple of hours of driving we arrived at our rural destination. The house we desired had more forest surrounding it than neighboring houses. It was located on the outskirts of a small mountain town. The house was two stories tall. Based upon the faded white paint covering cracked boards, I assumed it was old. I parked on the gravel driveway. Stepping out of the car, I was immediately greeted by the aroma of the woods.

The lights weren’t on and all the curtains were drawn. If the house had been disturbed in the last six months, there were no obvious signs of it. We approached the large hardwood door and I knocked. After a short wait, the man we were looking for opened the door. He looked to be in his early fifties. He was tall and thin, but broad shouldered. The hair that was missing from the top of his head had migrated to his face in an unkempt beard. His facial hair was soot black, peppered with grey, and looked to have not been trimmed in months. He was barefoot and wore a flannel shirt with slacks. I took the liberty of introducing the two of us, and Spencer began the questioning. “Mr. Beric, we were hoping to ask you some questions regarding your daughter.”

The man’s eyes darted between the two of us with suspicion. “You’re not with the police department are you?” He ascertained. “What do you want to know about Hailey?”

I was preparing an answer when Spencer stepped in. “I already know what the police know. As far as they’re concerned, the case is cold. But I think you can be more help to me than they would. And I also think I can be more help to you than the police were.”

This was obviously pouring salt in the man’s fresh wounds. “What are you talking about?” he demanded to know. “You better start explaining yourself right n-“

“Six months ago a stranger took your daughter from you.” Spencer interrupted. “I mean to find him, and kill him.”

Tears welled in the man’s eyes. He paused for a moment and invited us in. The interior of Mr. Beric’s house was as untouched as his hair, save for the silhouettes of numerous pictures now missing from the walls. We sat in a couch across from Mr. Beric who was seated in an armchair and looked as though he was being interviewed by ghosts. “Please, if you would, can you give your account on what happened to Hailey?” Spencer requested.

The man nervously bit his fingernails before responding. “When Hailey was born, her mother wanted nothing to do with her. I struggled, raising a child on my own. But Hailey always understood how hard it was for me.” The tears began again. “She really was the perfect daughter. Whenever I was wrestling with life she was the one part of if it that wasn’t difficult. She was always so well behaved. She loved music, reading, she painted, and she loved me. And that’s all I needed out of life. I could’ve been totally happy dying alone as long as Hailey still cared about me.” The man was trying to fight back his tears and was failing miserably. “And I really thought she did love me.” He sobbed.

“And then she just showed up one day with some boy you’d never even seen before.” Spencer said.

“I never even found out his name!” the father despaired, “Hailey just came home one day and told me she never wanted to see me again. She said she was going to live with her new boyfriend.” The man looked ready to vomit. “He had to have forced her to do it; to say all those terrible things. I don’t know how he threatened her or why, but that wasn’t my Hailey. She was never like that.”

“But where did they go?” Spencer asked. “Did they say where they were headed?” “The boy didn’t say a word the entire time he was here. They both just got in Hailey’s truck and left. I haven’t seen either of them, or the car, since.”

“But there was more to it than that.” Spencer insisted. “You said more to the police. What was it?”

“They…they said it was highly unlikely. They didn’t have any reason to…” The man then sighed. “After they left I tried to follow them. I got in my car, and I was able to keep up with them for a while, but eventually I lost them. But that’s what I don’t get. There’s only one place remotely close to where I lost the truck that they could have been going to.”

“So you do know where they went?” I asked.

“There’s a community bomb shelter in the forest,” he answered. “But I can’t imagine why they would ever go there. It’s been completely abandoned since the sixties. It was built into the side of the mountain deep in the forest. I mean, the police didn’t even think it was worth exploring. Only a handful of people know where it’s actually located.”

“And you’re one of those people.” Spencer looked almost euphoric.

“You really think there might be something there?” The faint sound of hope made its way into his voice. “If there is, we’re going to find it.” I assured him.

“You have to keep your promise,” Mr. Beric pleaded, “I’ll tell you where it is, but you have to promise me that if you can’t find my daughter, you’ll murder the son of a bitch who stole her from me.”

Spencer spent the whole ride there ranting about how sure he was that this was the lead he’d been waiting for and how everything fit. That didn’t surprise me. Spencer always performed every task with the dutiful enthusiasm of a dog with a bone. And this was the culmination of his life’s pursuit.

It was a long drive deep into the mountains through winding forest roads. The sun was setting as we approached our destination. I stopped the car in front of a dirt path blocked by a rusted chain that held up a “NO TRESPASSING” sign with pale faded letters. “This is it” he muttered as he exited the car. We walked past the sign and down the road for a while until Spencer stopped to his right. He cleared off some fallen leaves with his foot to reveal a narrow path diverging away from the road. Just where Hailey’s father had said it would be.

We trekked deeper and the sky darkened further as we were lost into the shadow created by the canopy of twisted trees. Each step in the crunching leaves was laced with caution as the slim trail grew more difficult to follow. As we trudged along into the dark deserted woods an eerie feeling came over me. I suppose that’s not to be unexpected when seeking out a living nightmare, but there was a distinct aura of uneasiness and ambiguity that made every bush and shadow in the dark a potential threat. As though the forest itself was watching me, and the thick expanse of trees that shot up like mangled black fingers worked in unison to conceal the sinister intentions that lurked beyond.

I tried to keep my mind off the chills running down my spine by talking to Spencer. “I don’t understand,” I told him, “If Charlotte influenced Hailey’s mind, then why go to her home in the first place? Why does she spend so much time manipulating her victims when she could make them go right to the trap?”

We stepped over a fallen tree and made our way around a corner before he gave me his answer. “Heartbreak.” He looked as pale as death. “I’ve asked myself the same thing and that’s the only answer I could conceive. She told so many needless lies, promised so many things, for seemingly no reason other than for the sake of betrayal. She never just deceives people, she toys with them. Maybe it’s something she needs to include in her process to feed, but I really believe she does it because she enjoys it. We’re not dealing with a mindless creature that does what it has to do to survive; she thrives off of deception and basks in your heartbreak.” He looked at me with the eyes of a wounded animal. “Do you want to know what the worst part of all of this is? I’ve given up my energy, all my money, and my life for this and the thing that eats me up the most is how much I miss her. After everything, I still lay awake at night wishing my wife was holding me. Killing her is the only chance I have left.”

I decided to stop talking after that. But silence meant my mind could only wander to the horrifying future. What was I even doing? Spencer was the brave one. If I hear a bump in the night I don’t explore it, I stay in bed. Leave it up to me to chicken out at the last minute. I wanted to turn back but Spencer needed me and I wasn’t going to let him down. But facing an ancient evil with only a briefcase to go off of? I tried to imagine what secret could lie within it. Maybe it could be some kind of ancient Indian sword, or ritual equipment for an exorcism, or maybe some hi-tech paranormal machine. All of it seemed unlikely. And of course there was the chance she wasn’t even in there. A million doubts flooded my mind but it was too late to dwell on them. If the directions were accurate, we were almost there.

The sky had darkened completely and I had been illuminating the way ahead of us with a headlamp I had brought with me. The side of the mountain came before us. The path abruptly ended to reveal nothing. There was no door, just dirt and rock. “Are we on the wrong path?” I asked in confusion.

“No” Spencer responded as resolute as ever. “It’s here.”

He ran his hands along the incline of the earth, clearing off deadfall until underneath it we heard the sound of metal scraping against metal. Spencer gasped and swept away debris to uncover a steel hatch. Without any hesitation Spencer tugged on the hatch; it was time. The door’s rusted hinges screeched in defiance. It swung wide, unearthing a pitch black tunnel that sat like a hole in the world.

Spencer’s face was a combination of intense fear and determination. He held out his briefcase and nodded. Slowly I took it from his hand and began the descent into the maw of oblivion. I ducked my head and crawled through the hatch. There was no time to think of how afraid I was.

Beneath the shelter’s entrance were a few small steps taking me to floor level. This bomb shelter seemed to be more like a buried metal cylinder than the concrete room I envisioned. Spencer stepped inside behind me. My small light fought to penetrate the darkness and I saw that all of the shelter’s walls were rounded but the floor was not. On the left side of the room were dozens of shelves stocked with canned food that expired decades ago. Running from along the length of the right wall were multiple beds.

I scoured the room for movement and found none. It wasn’t until my gaze swung to the far corner of the room that I saw it. A figure huddled in the dark. I froze. My stomach dropped and my heart was beating out of my chest. The figure was backed into the corner, shielding itself with skinny arms. It was hairless. Its skin was thin and dry as old leather. Its eyes weren’t open, thank god. But its mouth was contorted like it was giving a wordless cry of agony. I stood in terror, motionless. And so did the figure. “Is it…sleeping?” I asked Spencer as loud as I dared.

“No.” he replied. “It’s Hailey.”

I was rushing over to her when I heard the sound of the steel hatch slamming shut. I turned around looking for Charlotte and saw Spencer standing in front of me. My eyes met his and a slight grin spread across his face. Then he shrieked. It was a high thin shriek. Like the rasp of a dying man wheezing for his last breath. He threw his head back, and his hair melted into his pores. His flesh pulled against his skeleton, distorting him into a mass of writhing limbs. Desperately, I fumbled with the latches of the briefcase and when it finally ripped open, I could only gape in horror as stacks of phone books tumbled to the ground. Unable to move, I saw the color in Spencer’s eyes darken in shade. They changed from grey, to black, to nothingness….
